sentences.text: Harpachochampsa is a poorly known extinct crocodilian genus found at the Bullock Creek fossil site in the Northern Territory of Australia.
The known specimen includes a partial skull and fragments of a thin snout that resembles that of the false gharial, indicating it was a fish-eater.
This animal was pseudoheterodont, meaning its premaxillary teeth varied greatly in size while its maxillary teeth were more uniform.
The only preserved functional premaxillary tooth faced slightly outward instead of straight down.
Harpachochampsa had roughly circular premaxillae containing five teeth on each side, separated from maxillary teeth by a notch likely for an enlarged lower jaw tooth.
Unlike other crocodylids where the fifth maxillary tooth is largest, the fourth premaxillary tooth was the largest in Harpacochampsa.
The genus Harpacochampsa was described by Megirian, Murray, and Willis in 1991.
The genus name Harpacochampsa combines Greek words meaning 'to seize' and 'crocodile,' referencing the specialized premaxillary teeth.
Harpachochampsa likely primarily ate fish and turtles, but its stout build suggests it may have also hunted medium-sized mammals.
Its elongated snout indicates that Harpacochampsa was a piscivore in life.
Harpachochampsa is classified in the family Crocodylidae and belongs to the parent group Gavialoidea.

The subfamily classification for Harpacochampsa is uncertain and listed as Mekosuchinae with question marks, though some experts disagree because it might be the only known mekosuchine with a long, thin snout.
Harpachochampsa lived during the Early Miocene epoch, specifically from the Langhian to the Serravallian stages, between 15.98 and 11.63 million years ago.

It is debated whether Harpacochampsa belongs to the Mekosuchinae, is a basal crocodyloid, or is a type of gavialid. The classification of Harpacochampsa within Mekosuchinae has been questioned by various authors, making its exact position controversial. Ristevski et al. (2021) recovered Harpacochampsa as one of the basalmost crocodyloids, neither a mekosuchine nor a gavialoid.
